en: The Original Meaning of the Treasure Mirror Samādhi, Explained by Jingxi [Zhanran]. Composed by Xingce.
Regarding the Treasure Mirror Samādhi: it is that which Dongshan personally received as a seal from Yunyan and secretly transmitted to Caoshan. Dongshan...

The masters of later generations feared that [this teaching] might fall into public circulation; they therefore transmitted it secretly within their chambers to establish the definitive tenets and prevent its leakage.
It was only after Zhu Shiying obtained it from the old monk that it first became available for transmission to the world.

The text consists of three hundred and sixty words, among which several phrases—such as "separating the six lines" (*liu yao*), "partiality and correctness" (*pian zheng*), and "reciprocal interaction" (*hui hu*)—serve as the pivotal axis of the entire work. Nevertheless...

The secret treasury is a profound bolt that is difficult to open; though there have been one or two venerable masters who have attempted to clarify its meaning, they have instead produced fragmented interpretations that miss the essential intent.

This has served only to disgrace the ancestral tradition and mislead future students. Recently, I observed the work *Rendian Yimou* (The Eyes of Humanity and Heaven), which records the tenets of the Five Houses;
therein, the errors and corruptions within the Caodong school are particularly numerous. Is this not due to being deluded regarding this fundamental samādhi?
For this reason, my friend, the Layman Lvtang (Hu Jie), saw it and was pained by it; he commissioned me to examine and rectify its meaning.

Shortly thereafter, the Layman passed away. I kept this matter within my breast for several years. One day, upon being unexpectedly exhorted by a Zen practitioner, I closed my door, burned incense, and recited the late master’s words three times.
Therein, I realized the profound significance of the *samādhi* within the "double li" hexagram.
Within the hexagram, insights appear repeatedly and in layers; therefore, I have extracted and unraveled their threads to compose six types of diagrams and expositions to elucidate them.
The first is general, while the latter five are specific. This is intended to reveal what is subtle and profound, rather than for mere worldly dissemination.

I am aware of my transgressions, yet I have no leisure to deliberate upon them. Having lamented that ancient expositions are erroneous, and unwilling to betray the trust placed in me by Lü Tang, I have exerted myself to compose this.
How dare I claim that the fundamental meaning of Samādhi is truly as I have set forth it? Only those with the discerning eye shall judge it.
As for the six types of diagrammatic expositions, they are: the *Diagrammatic Exposition of the Treasure Mirror Samādhi* and the *Diagram of the Interchange of Orthodoxy and Deviation*.

1. Explanation of the Threefold Layered Diagram of the Trigrams; 2. Explanation of the Diagram of the Five Transformations Establishing Positions; 3. Explanation of the Diagram of Analogies Revealing the Dharma;
4. Explanation of the Diagram of the Six Lines Encompassing Meaning.

The Explanation of the Diagram of the Treasure Mirror Samādhi concerns the single aperture of the ultimate direction, which has not been transmitted by the thousand sages. Because it follows the *siddhānta* according to its meaning, it is thus manifested in patterns and colors.

In the Vehicle of Confucianism, this is called the Great Ultimate (*tài jí*). Originally it cannot be named, yet it is forcibly named the Great Ultimate; originally it cannot be described, yet this form is forcibly fashioned for it.
All things, from the two polarities and the four images up to the sixty-four hexagrams, are produced from this.

This mutual production arises from non-characteristic (animitta); where there is no characteristic, there is no production, yet nothing is not produced. Now, discussing this characteristic, it has various names within my Dharma:
the *Avataṃsaka* calls it the "One True Dharma-realm" (*eka-dharmadhātu*), and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* calls it the "One Real Characteristic" (*eka-bhūtalakṣaṇa*). The *Nirvāṇa*...
This is called the Secret Treasury (*guhyagarbha*). All sentient beings of the six realms possess this and are obscured by it;
as the eighth *ālayavijñāna*, it is called the nature of the *tathāgatagarbha*. The Buddhas of the three periods of time transform this and realize this;

as the ninth *amala-vijñāna*, it is called the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*). The ancestral masters of successive generations awaken to this and transmit this; it is the Most Supreme Secret School.

The essential meaning is called the Treasure Mirror Samādhi. All vehicles of teaching (*śāsana-yāna*) serve as the means of expression (*vyañjaka*), while this [Samādhi] is that which is expressed (*vyaṅgya*).
All vehicles of doctrine (*siddhānta-yāna*) serve as the indicators, while this is that which is indicated. Nevertheless, within this, there is neither subject nor object, nor name or characteristic.
The wordless phrase: this is what is called when chaos has not yet divided and black and white have not yet manifested. A superior person who investigates the profound must first realize this.
If one has not realized this yet speaks of the orthodox or the deviant, of the luminous or the obscure, it is like talking about the moon;

how could it illuminate the objective realm? Therefore, know that such a person deviates from the essence of luminous purity and lacks the function of discerning reflection. Even if they were to gaze within a precious mirror all day long...
Yet, samādhi cannot be attained. Nevertheless, even when one produces such signs, it already belongs to the defiled; how much more so in the case of *pohua* (confusion/obfuscation)?
Let us set that aside for now and discuss the diagrams of the "Correct" and "Partial" as they interact and transform.
In this diagram, the Two Polarities (liangyi) have been distinguished and black and white have already been divided. Black represents the orthodox (zheng), while white represents the biased (pian).
This refers to the principle that within the orthodox there is the biased, and within the biased there is the orthodox; the meaning of their mutual interpenetration (huixu) originates here.

That there remains a single void-mark (xushang) in the center represents the matter of transcending [the dualities]; it is now likewise hidden between the black and the white. Black and white represent the two—odd and even.
The "Number" (shù) arises from the aforementioned characteristics of the Great Ultimate (Tàijí). It serves as the foundation for the hexagrams, lines, and images.

However, when discussing the principles manifested therein, they are not limited to the categories of biased and correct alone. Here, I shall briefly correlate names and meanings so that one does not lose sight of the fundamental tenet. Specifically, "Black" (hēi) signifies correctness in terms of position;

it signifies darkness in terms of appearance; it signifies night in terms of temporal division; it signifies the interior in terms of spatial location; and in terms of human relations, it signifies...
The Lord and Father: he represents the sovereign of the two families; he represents the principle within the dharma-realm; he represents the essence within the dharma-gates;

he represents the nature within the two virtues; he represents wisdom within the two adornments; he represents reality within the two knowledges; he represents the source within the two gates; and he represents the fruition within the forty-two stages.
That which is called "white" signifies the partial stage, the characteristic of illumination, the division of day, and the external realm.

They serve as ministers and sons; as guests in households; as the functioning of the dharma-realm; as the gate of utility; as the cultivation of virtue; as the movement of merit; as skillful means and wisdom;

as the gate of traces; and as the stage of cause. Although these various pairs of dharmas each abide according to their respective positions, they interpenetrate one another through their flight, concealment, and manifestation.
Yet, despite this mutual interpenetration, each remains in its original position, never becoming confused with the other.

This is not an object of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is such when entering this samādhi, this principle of mutual interpenetration constitutes the essential tenet of our school.
Students of the Caodong lineage (*Dòngzōng*) should especially examine this in detail.
The Explanation of the Diagram of the Threefold Division of the Hexagrams:
The general meaning of this diagram has already been briefly seen. Each hexagram consists of six lines (*yao*), which are fundamentally comprised of only two numbers: the odd and the even.

The former sages took their "reciprocal and interchanging" imagery to establish the fundamental principles. However, because these principles are both profound and secret, those expressed through written texts...
Furthermore, [the text] cites [these points] but does not resolve them, intending for students to reflect deeply upon them and realize them for themselves after entering the Way.
Consequently, various masters of the past have offered conflicting interpretations, muddling the meaning of the "three repetitions and five transformations.

They diverge from the original hexagram to separately transform five other hexagrams, providing fragmented and forced explanations that greatly miss the essential intent. This fails to recognize that the original text simply states: "As follows... (如).
The separation from the six lines takes up the imagery of the interaction between the orthodox and the biased; it does not take up the meaning of the *Li* hexagram as the trigram of the heart-fire.
Within the fundamental hexagram itself, there naturally exists the wondrous interest of the three layers and five transformations formed by Heaven.
If a student does not seek elsewhere, but instead contemplates these line-images with close observation and thorough playfulness, thinking upon them, thinking again, and thinking yet more deeply—
If one does so, then the spirits will provide a mysterious communication and the intention of the patriarchs will be fully realized without any remaining obscurity.

Now, rather than attacking heterodox views, I shall directly set forth the fundamental meaning. First, the six lines of the original hexagram are divided into three layers to symbolize the three virtues—this is what is meant by "layering them into three.
Specifically, the first and second lines constitute the first layer. The school of Dongshan prizes...

Through mutual interpenetration (*huìhù*), the *xiàng* (image) of "following" represents the "central with partiality" (*zhèng zhōngpiān*), while the *xiàng* of "interpenetration" represents the "partial with centrality" (*piān zhōngzhèng*).
This is identical to the first and second changes among the five changes of the central hexagram. This image represents the virtue of *prajñā*.

Taking the third and fourth lines as a double layer and observing them through mutual interpenetration, there is pure yang with no yin; however, the fourth line is yang occupying a yin position, which constitutes the subtle harmony between the central and the partial. Therefore...
The image of "coming from the center" corresponds to the hexagram lines of the third transformation; this image represents the virtue of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

By taking the two lines of the fifth and sixth positions as the threefold repetition, the interlocking image is "reaching the center," and the sequential image is "arriving at the center. These are identical to the two transformed lines of the fourth and fifth positions;

this image represents the virtue of liberation (*vimuktikāya*). Furthermore, the three lines of the inner trigram, with their fixed positions of yin and yang, represent self-enjoyment (*svasaṃbhogakāya*).
Samādhi. When the three lines of the outer hexagram have their yin and yang positions exchanged, it becomes the Samādhi of Other-Enjoyment.
The meaning of these three types of virtuous samādhis shall be explained extensively later.

The Diagram of the Five Changes and Positions explains that these three layers of six lines transform into five positions, thereby exhausting the principles of a single hexagram; this is what is meant by "the changes being exhausted, the five [positions] are formed.
Within these five positions, they are further divided into ten lines, which take their images from one another in alternating succession. Therefore...
It still does not go beyond the six lines of the original hexagram. Is not the subtlety of layered transformation found therein?
However, there are two meanings of "change" (*bian*): first, the meaning of transformation (*bianhua*); second, the meaning of alteration (*bianyi*). Here we take only the meaning of alteration.

For example, the mutual exchange of cause and effect across the forty-two stages—what is called "altered birth-and-death" (*bianyi shengsi*)—is precisely this. Since one now knows that change carries the sense of alteration, [the principle is established].
Thus, it is the lines (*xiāo*) of the *Yī* that change, not the trigrams (*guǎ*). To separately produce five additional trigrams has no connection to the names or meanings of the five positions;

moreover, their sequence is disordered and they do not accord with the diagrams. This is truly a case of extreme thoughtlessness. Furthermore, it is clearly stated that the six lines of the *Lí* trigram undergo "partiality," "correctness," "reversion," and "interchange.
Why then resort to multiple trigrams and multiple lines? The root of this ailment that has plagued the ages lies solely in misinterpreting "change" (*biàn*).
It all results in "five" and "one line" alone. Dongshan’s original intention was that by changing the six lines, one exactly forms the five positions (*wuwei*).
However, he mistakenly changed "changing to the end" (*yijing*) to "transforming to the end" (*huajing*), and further mistakenly changed "forming the five positions" to "forming the five hexagrams.

Consequently, his fragmented interpretations became increasingly elaborate and increasingly erroneous. This concludes the brief clarification of the five transformations. Furthermore, if one wishes to correlate the positions, it is unnecessary—

Taking ten lines from one another, we focus solely on the six lines; the meaning of the five positions is already complete therein. Now, let us further clarify this: the first line is taken as "the Center within Partiality.
This is because the entirety of Principle (li) is itself Phenomena (shi); therefore, within this very Center there is partiality.

However, the marks of partiality cannot be seen—just like the moon on the first day of the lunar month. Although its luminous aspect cannot be said to be absent in the darkness, it is not manifest. Thus, the *Cantong qi* says: [The moon] is like the first day of the month... [it is] hidden in the dark.
The *Qiyun* says: "There is brightness within darkness; do not seek it by looking for the appearance of brightness.
For this reason, there is no need to take the second *yin* line from elsewhere. Next, the second single line is taken as "central and correct within partiality" (*piānzhōng zhèng*).

This is because the entirety of phenomena is itself the principle; thus, within this partiality there is correctness. However, the appearance of correctness cannot be seen, just like [the sun] on the day of the full moon.
In the moon, the aspect of darkness is definitively present within the light; thus, the *Cantong qi* says:
"When there is darkness within the light, do not encounter it with darkness. For this reason, it is unnecessary to mutually take the third yang line.
Next, the two lines of the fourth and third positions are taken as coming from the center; this position must necessarily have both lines mutually taken to form the position.

The meaning [of these terms] shall be explained separately later. Next, the fifth single line is taken as "reaching the center through integration" (jiānzhōng zhì), and the sixth single line is taken as "arriving at the center through integration" (jiānzhōng dào).
This is because these two positions follow "wondrous harmony" (miàoyè) in the central position;

therefore, although the two diagrams consist respectively of pure white and pure black, one represents wondrous harmony manifesting in function, whereby principle and phenomena are both revealed, while the other represents wondrous harmony... [text truncated].

They return to the essence, wherein both principle and phenomena are simultaneously extinguished; this is called "reaching through integration" (*jiānzhì*) or "reaching through integration" (*jiāndào*).

"Integration" (*jiān*) carries the meaning of mutual interpenetration. For this reason, it is unnecessary to separately select the fourth and fifth lines. Since this is so, why is it that within the "repeated transformations" (*diébiàn*), one always selects the double lines and not the single lines?
It is because although the meaning of the single lines is complete, their characteristics (*xiàng*) are not manifest; thus, the image of "returning and interpenetrating" (*huíhù*) is not apparent.
This becomes clearly and brilliantly manifest. Furthermore, it differs from the single position of "Coming from the Center" in terms of being singular or multiple.
For this reason, the singular is set aside and the multiple is employed. However, speaking according to reality, every position is interpenetrating and every hexagram-line is interpenetrating;

the singular contains the multiple, and the multiple is itself the singular. Thus, the mutual transformation of the singular and multiple further reveals the meaning of the infinitely layered and inexhaustible. Contemplate this.
...it. These two metaphors clarify the Dharma;

the explanation of this diagram’s principle is even more subtle than the previous one. The former allocated positions based on the primary and secondary, as well as the single and the combined; now it is based on the totality.

The distinction between the broad and the narrow reveals the Dharma; the general and the specific reveal the flavor of the Dharma, while the broad and the narrow reveal the characteristics of the Dharma.
This is like the taste of a *kṣavaka* herb, or like a vajra-pestle. By means of these two metaphors, the dharmas of the five stages are revealed together.
This is called "the mystery within mysteries, the gate of all wonders. Now, to first clarify the general and the specific:
in the analogy, the *chí-cǎo* (barberry) is the general, while the five flavors are the specific. In the Dharma, the hexagram *Lí* (Fire) is the general, while the five positions are the specific.

The *chí-cǎo* is the *wù-wèi-zǐ* (Chinese magnolia fruit) among medicinal herbs; that one substance possesses five flavors serves as a metaphor for how one hexagram possesses five positions. This is the opening.
One becomes five; the five combined become one. When the attachment to "one" and "five" vanishes, opening and closing [the gates] are unimpeded.
The general meaning is as follows. To explain it in sequential order: Heaven, the first creative force (*qian*), generates Water, which constitutes the first line (*yao*) in the position of Yang.

Water is said to "moisten and flow downward. This symbolizes the first line residing at the bottom of a hexagram. Moistening and flowing downward produces saltiness; therefore, it represents the flavor of salt. Earth, the second creative force (*kun*), generates Fire. This is...

The second line represents a yin position. Fire is said to "flame upward," which symbolizes the second line rising from below; as flaming upward produces bitterness, it corresponds to the flavor of bitterness.
Heaven-three generates wood, which constitutes the fifth line, a yang position. Wood is said to be "curved and straight"; curvature and straightness are opposites.
This symbolizes that the fifth yin line is the opposite of the yang position; as curved and straight produce sourness, it corresponds to the flavor of sourness.

Furthermore, the Earth produces four types of metal, which constitute the six yin positions of the hexagram lines. Metal is called "following transformation" (*cong ge*). "Following" (*cong*) and "transformation" (*ge*) are opposites;
this symbolizes that the sixth yang line is opposite to the yin position. "Following transformation" produces pungency; therefore, it represents the flavor of pungency.

Heaven produces five types of earth, which constitutes the central yang position. Regarding earth, there is "planting and reaping" (*jia sai*). This symbolizes that, like the ground, it can produce all manner of meritorious virtues. Planting...

Harvesting produces sweetness; thus it represents the flavor of sweetness. Furthermore, water takes moisture as its meaning, symbolizing the initial slight wetting at the beginning of the "central line being biased" (zhèng zhōng piān).
Fire takes illumination as its meaning, symbolizing the commencement of practice toward the fruit at the beginning of the "biased line being central" (piān zhōng zhèng).

Wood takes growth as its meaning, symbolizing the manifestation of function when both [central and biased] reach their culmination. Metal takes withdrawal and concealment as its meaning, symbolizing the [beginning of the] "biased line being central."
Upon reaching [the state of] *zhì* (知), one returns to the essence (*tǐ*). Earth takes solidity and stillness as its defining meaning; yet, within it lies wisdom that vibrates.

The hexagram *Zhèng* (中) emerges from this, representing the intention of subtle movement within the solid reality of the double yang lines. Thus, by means of the Five Elements, it is correlated with the five positions of flavor.
Furthermore, among these five elements, water and fire are opposites, as are metal and wood; earth alone has no opposite and occupies the central position.

Symbolizing that which comes from the center, it wondrously embraces the four surrounding positions. Occupying the central and upright position alone, it holds a place of supreme dignity and must not have an opposite.
Thus, in the verses of Dongshan, he cautioned students not to "touch upon the current taboo."

This means that if one treats it with respectful care, there will be auspiciousness. Furthermore, in the analogy, the single flavor encountered is complete with all five flavors because they are, in total, one substance.
In the Dharma, as soon as a single position is raised, all five positions are encompassed because they collectively belong to the One Mind.
Therefore, the *tṛṇa* grass is borrowed as a metaphor for the wondrous flavor of the Dharma. Next, to clarify the breadth and narrowness: in the analogy...

The broadness and narrowness [of this form] are easy to understand. As for the *vajra*, it is the precious mace wielded by a powerful warrior; its shape is broad at the head and tail while the waist alone is narrow.
Therefore, it is taken as a metaphor for the characteristics of the Dharma (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). Regarding the broadness and narrowness within the Dharma:

although the six lines of the *Chongli* hexagram are divided into five positions, they do not deviate from the three principles (*tridharma*). Thus, the first and second lines are combined to constitute a single principle. This is because of the underlying logic (*li*).

Phenomena correspond to affairs; wisdom corresponds to practice. They are like the two wings of a bird or the two wheels of a chariot. One desires the wings to be balanced and the wheels to be aligned;

if either is lacking, it is difficult to soar through the sky or travel far. Therefore, although the hexagram lines and positions have a sequential order, the characteristics of the Dharma have no before or after.
When these two positions are simultaneously fused, this is true Prajñā. This is what is meant by "the breadth of the head within the Dharma. Next...
The fourth and fifth positions are combined into a single dharma. This is because essence (*tǐ*) corresponds to function (*yòng*), and expedient means (*quán*) corresponds to reality (*shí*).

It is like the moon having its reflection, or a lamp having its light: when they manifest, both manifest together; when they subside, both subside together. To separate them results in deluded views and frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*).
Therefore, although the hexagram lines and positions have a sequential order, the characteristics of the dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) have no before or after; the two positions are simultaneous.
This is true liberation; this is the "tail" (the conclusion) within the Dharma. Next, the third position, that of the Center from Which All Comes, constitutes a single dharma of its own.
This is because the two preceding positions are those that enter by looking toward this position, while the two subsequent positions are those that emerge by turning away from it.
Only this position governs what precedes and encompasses what follows; it stands alone without peer, as the unity of principle and phenomenon, wisdom and practice, essence and function.
Regarding provisional and ultimate [truth]: upon entering this stage, all are entirely suchness (tathatā). That is to say, there is one suchness and no second suchness.
Because there is no second suchness, it is the true Dharmakāya; this constitutes the "narrow waist" within the Dharma. Furthermore, it is likened to a precious vajra-pestle:
if the head is lifted, the waist and tail follow along; if the waist is lifted, both head and tail come with it; and the same applies if the tail is lifted. These three parts are as one.
If it is broken, it does not become a vajra. Within the Dharma, these three dharmas are in fact one dharma; this is called the "Secret Treasury" (*guhyakośa*).
If we refer to its original name, it inherently possesses both the dharma and the metaphor, and is thus named the "Treasure Mirror Samādhi" (*ratnādarśa-samādhi*).

Herein, the correct and the partial are explained: true *prajñā* must necessarily possess liberation and the *dharmakāya*. When explaining the correct [aspect], the true *dharmakāya* must necessarily possess *prajñā* and liberation. This explains them as being concurrent.
The center is likewise true liberation. If even one of these three dharmas is lacking, the secret treasury (guhyagarbha) is not established.
Furthermore, in the analogy, the precious pestle is a vajra; because it is firm and indestructible, it ultimately possesses the characteristics of both breadth and narrowness.
In the Dharma, the secret treasury is the Jewel Mirror Samādhi; because it is perfectly pure and without deficiency, it ultimately possesses the marks of both breadth and narrowness. Therefore...
The borrowing of the vajra serves as a metaphor for the wondrous nature of dharmalakṣaṇa. Furthermore, one should understand the characteristics of opening and closing within this samādhi:
first, a single hexagram is divided into three layers; next, these three layers are transformed into five positions; now, these five positions are condensed into three dharmas;
and finally, these three dharmas are fused back into a single dharma. Yet, this samādhi is neither one nor three.
It is not five; it is five, three, and one. By layering these, they form three, clarifying that one is three. When transformed to their limit, they become five, clarifying that one is five.
Like the taste of the *kṣavaka* grass, it proves that five is one. Like the vajra scepter, it proves that three is one.
Extending even further, it is neither opening nor closing, neither total nor partial, neither broad nor narrow—it is precisely opening.
It is both unified and comprehensive; it is both general and particular; it is both expansive and narrow. This is called the Great Samādhi; this is called the Profound Samādhi;
this is called the Inconceivable Samādhi. Furthermore, within a single hexagram, the five positions interact to yield ten lines.

While the preceding and succeeding four positions share the same imagery yet differ in meaning, in the two positions of the Correct and the Biased, the lower line serves as the primary element and the upper line serves as the interactive element.
Upon reaching the two positions [of the second and third hexagrams], the upper line is taken as the primary and the lower line as the interlocking (hu).
This is what those who contemplate the images (*xiang*) must fully understand. The fundamental meaning has already been clarified; I shall briefly critique divergent interpretations.

Juefan altered five hexagrams—*Daguò*, *Zhōngfú*, *Xùn*, *Duì*, and the doubled *Lí*—and further changed "reaching the center by means of both" (*jiān zhōng zhì*) to "reaching the center by means of one side" (*piān zhōng zhì*), in order to contrast it with "coming from the center" (*zhèng zhōng lái*). By using "both" (*jiān*)...
The case of "Arriving at the One Who Dwells Alone" has subsequently caused great confusion among scholars; it must be clarified.

This "One Who Comes from the Center" is naturally noble and sovereign, serving as the pivotal axis for the other four positions, just as earth is the central element among the five phases within the five directions.
How could there possibly be a counterpart? Furthermore, the image of "coming from the center" is a black mark within a circle, while "reaching from the partial" is a purely white mark;
these two do not correspond at all. Moreover, "arriving at the combined" is a purely black mark, which directly corresponds to the purely white mark of "reaching from the combined.
How can it be said that the single position of "arriving at the combined" stands alone at the end without a counterpart?
Furthermore, if one takes the "partial" [line] to correspond with the "central" [position], then there would be two positions within the center, which contradicts the analogy of the pestle's shape.

Moreover, if one assigns the five hexagrams to the five positions, then the five positions would not be fully contained within a single hexagram, which violates the analogy of the taste of the *zhicǎo* herb.
This would then be entirely inconsistent with both the Five Diagrams and the Two Parables, and would completely obscure the essential meaning of the five stages (*wuwei*).

Since Juefan erroneously produced the "five hexagrams" and further claimed that the ancient masters and great monks all employed the "Arrival within the Intermediate" (*jianzhongzhi*), one does not understand what his meaning was.
Truly, it is as the saying goes: "Before the eyes of one with clear vision, there is three feet of darkness. This is indeed so. Furthermore, Master Yongjue [altered]...
Regarding the five hexagrams of Jiji (Already Crossed), Weiji (Not Yet Crossed), Sun (Diminution), Yi (Increase), and Zhongli (Double Li):

although the five positions they occupy roughly accord with the characteristics of the phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), in these two [hexagrams], the ultimate positions are placed below while the positions of the correct and biased are placed above. This results from the four hexagrams being transposed and rearranged;
thus, according to their assigned positions within the hexagrams, the beginning and end are inverted. Though this may appear similar, it is in fact profoundly erroneous. Alas! These two elders—

He is indeed what is called a great elder; yet, regarding the subtlety of his layered transformations and the excellence of his two metaphors, there remains that which he has not yet fully understood.
As for those of inferior intellect and limited comprehension, there is no need to discuss them further.
**Explanatory Diagram of the Six Lines: Questions and Answers** Question:
As for the five types of diagrams explained above, they are sufficient to elucidate the wondrous meaning of samādhi.

Why, then, has this one been composed? Answer: There are two purposes. First, it is to enlighten the ignorant; second, it is to synthesize the essential meanings. This is because the knowledge and understanding [of some] are dim and superficial.
Such a person claims not to be attached to words and symbols and does not seek a profound understanding; consequently, they do not taste even a single drop from this ocean of profound meaning.
Their intention is this: "The six lines of the hexagram *Chongli* (the Double Li) were merely metaphors incidentally entrusted to us by the ancient sages.

Why must one investigate them with such precision and seek their depths? If this were truly the case, then why is it that the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the king of all scriptures, is found everywhere [to teach these principles]?

This expresses the Dharma. The Elder Fangshan composed this treatise, frequently employing the principles of the Eight Trigrams (*bagua*), the Five Elements (*wuxing*), and Yin-Yang to provide explanations.
How could all of these have arisen by mere chance? Furthermore, did the River not spontaneously produce the diagrams, and did the Luo River not spontaneously produce the writings?
Did Fuxi not spontaneously draw the trigrams and their numbers? Could it be that the Sage arbitrarily attached words and images for one to speculate upon? Since...
This is no mere coincidence. Within this single hexagram of the double Li (☲☲), all phenomena of both the mundane and supramundane realms are perfectly and completely contained.

Were one to extensively encompass its categories of meaning, the fundamental principles of all Buddhist teachings and the essential tenets of the various ancestral schools would be fully exhausted without exception.

For now, I shall briefly summarize the main outlines so that those who have not yet understood may gain some knowledge of the boundaries of the meanings of the six lines. If one can then divine and clarify them through spiritual insight— [The text continues with the hexagram analysis.]
To extend this principle to all its categories depends upon the individual. A brief explanation of the categories of meaning thus subsumed is as follows:
First, taking the three lines of the inner trigram (*neigua*) as representing the samādhi of self-enjoyment—this is because the first line occupies a position of pure yang.
If one correlates this with the teachings of the vehicles (*jiao-cheng*), it symbolizes Mañjuśrī’s fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) at the inception of the Dharma, such as when Sudhana was a youth.
For those of pure yang, seeing Mañjuśrī at the outset is like meeting a friend of pure yang; they suddenly clarify the fundamental principle and give rise to the bodhicitta.
Thus, he is the wisdom that serves as the root for the beginner's mind. Within the five chapters of the *Tiantai Mohe Zhiguan*, this corresponds to the "Arousing the Great Mind.
If we consider the traces of the Master’s [Śākyamuni’s] single-period of teaching, it corresponds to his birth in the royal palace.

Regarding the signs of the initial descent: if a student of the Way first gives rise to the aspiration for enlightenment, deeply mindful of birth and death, and encounters a true spiritual friend who reveals that which lies prior to the formation of body, mind, and the world—such that their single eye suddenly opens and they instantly clarify what is inherently possessed—this is assigned to this stage.
If one aligns this with the various patriarchs, it corresponds to being born into the house of the Dharma King; therefore, it is [the stage of]...
The Prince is born. Having long turned his back on awakening, he now for the first time accords with it;
thus, toward the true, eternal principle that has existed since beginningless time, he now suddenly opens it through the power of wisdom. This is called "the partial within the central.
It means that inverted perceptions are extinguished and one sincerely grants oneself permission [to proceed].
The second line is a yin line occupying a yin position. Its image represents the vast practice of Samantabhadra prior to the Path, encompassing the meritorious achievements of the fifty-two stages.

It is like Sudhana, who, after realizing the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) atop Mount Sumeru, subsequently traveled through one hundred and ten cities to attend upon fifty-three spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), penetrating each of their diverse gateways and teachings one by one; this is called traversing great meritorious achievements.

Within the five chapters on *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, this corresponds to the stage of "Practicing Great Conduct. If we refer to the Original Teacher, this represents the aspect of his ascetic practices after leaving the household life.
It refers to those practitioners who, after attaining awakening, tread this path without being satisfied with minor gains;

they undergo multifaceted refinement in the forge of the masters, deeply clarifying the distinctions [of phenomena] until their realization becomes increasingly profound and esoteric. Such individuals are assigned to this stage.
If one synthesizes the various patriarchs, this constitutes the completion of the great enterprise by traversing all stages; thus it is called "Born at Court" (Chao-sheng).

However, its meaning differs slightly from that of Shi-shuang’s verse. That [case] refers to the "external succession" of the ministerial lineage who does not occupy the throne, whereas this refers to the "internal succession" of the royal lineage who likewise has not yet occupied the throne.
Furthermore, because one advances through each stage without turning back, it is called "Serving" (Feng); [this applies to] each and every stage.
Because one proceeds toward the ultimate fruit by means of non-abiding practice, it is called "the rectification of the partial.

This refers to the fact that even a difference as slight as a hair’s breadth would fail to correspond with the musical scales (*lüyǔ*). Thus, in these two stages, wisdom and practice mutually support one another, and merit and position advance alternately.
When wisdom attains practice, its great functions flourish; when practice attains wisdom, every thought-moment is non-active (*wuwei*). One is two, and two are one; they are not merely one.
Non-dual yet one, and yet two; thus, the virtue of *prajñā* is perfected.
Fearing that students might lose their illumination upon reaching this point, the first hexagram is taken and its upper and lower lines are interchanged to reveal the subtlety of causal wisdom.
This is what is meant by "neither turning away from nor touching," like a great mass of fire.
The third line is also yang occupying a yang position. Its image represents the subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) after having realized equal enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Having inherited the preceding stage by means of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) to advance in great practice and reach the ultimate fruit, both the person and the position are correct.

Combining this with the previous two positions, it symbolizes the practitioner who has entered from the mundane into the sacred, wandering extensively through the ocean of fruition, flowing into the center of the center, never regressing.
It does not abide. Upon reaching this point, one turns one's merit toward the ultimate station; as the practice for self-benefit is fulfilled, it constitutes the samādhi of self-enjoyment.
It is like Sudhana’s southern pilgrimage, which culminates at Maitreya’s tower: without leaving his current location, he has visited all [the teachers];

without departing from a single mind, his journey is complete. In a single lifetime, he perfectly realizes the fruit of Buddhahood, instantly transcending the three great eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*) through the integration of principle and phenomena.

Being thus one and the same, with both essence and function being correct, this is the wisdom that reaches the other shore. Within the five chapters on *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, it is said that one shall realize the great fruit.

If we consider it according to our Original Teacher, it represents the state of attaining enlightenment beneath the tree. The student directly realizes the single mind (*ekacitta*) and does not harbor any state of awakening;
they penetrate to the very source of all phenomena and pass through the final, secure barrier. This is what is meant by "the study of a lifetime."
Those for whom the task is completed are assigned to this hexagram. If one aligns this with the various patriarchs, this represents the final body of Equal Enlightenment;
thus it is called the "last birth. Because one arrives there by means of great meritorious achievements, it is termed "merit"—specifically, merit within the midst [of the path].
This is what is meant by the saying: "When categories are not uniform, they are known through their convergence. Now, this "last-born prince" herein is identical to Dongshan’s "exact center."
The origins of these two are different. This [the "coming from the center"] refers to one who has long accumulated merit and only then enters the position;
that [the "coming from the side"] refers to one who is already established in the correct position and undergoes a transformation of the body.

It must be understood that the single position of "coming from the center" is named based on the image of the fourth line above, which is taken as the intended meaning within the third transformation of the interchanging lines (*xiāng*). Although these three lines are correct, [the former]...

Because there is no meaning of "coming," "coming" is precisely the coming of the Tathāgata. To say he "comes by means of True Suchness" (tathatā) means he comes from the sublime harmony within the Center.
Therefore, it is called "coming from the Center. Because he comes from the Center, he is not like those born at the periphery who have not yet left the Center;
nor is it a matter of arriving simultaneously with them. As Dongshan’s verse says: "Within non-existence there is a path, yet it is separated by dust and grime. There is no...
This "Middle" is the path of true existence from which one comes; as it has not yet departed from its station, it remains separated from dust and grime.

Those who do not penetrate this mistake it for having transcended dust and grime; a single character’s error thus leads them to conflate it with the subsequent stage. Dongshan’s establishment of these words is so subtle and wondrous.
Yet, while the masters of the past have sometimes equated it with the "last-born" or versified it as a functional achievement, none of them have grasped it correctly.

The essential point is this: in antiquity, there was only Cao Shan who personally received the oral instructions from [Dongshan]. Therefore, his Five Ranks Verses captured the very marrow of Dongshan’s teaching.
Regarding the verse on "Coming from the Center," it says: "Without leaving the Tushita realm, the black hen walks upon the snow. Those who misunderstand this say:

The black hen represents the orthodox; the snow represents the deviant. This is the turning of the position to accord with function: one benefits sentient beings and receives things while situated within the deviant position;
hence it is called "walking upon the snow. Furthermore, regarding the diagrammatic evidence of the error:

the reason the diagram has the interior black and the exterior white is precisely the image of the black hen on the snow. If this is so, how does it differ from the "Arriving in the Simultaneous" (jiānzhōng zhì)? Moreover—
Since it is said that he has not yet left the Tuṣita realm, how could he be walking upon white snow?
One must understand that the intent of Caoshan’s verse uses the black chicken to represent the person. The snow and the Tuṣita realm both symbolize the "correct position" (zhengwei).

Here, "snow" takes the meaning of "a single color" rather than the meaning of "white. As the verse further states, "Cold ice forms within the flames," where "flames" take the meaning of "clarity" to represent the "partial" (pian).

The color red is not taken [to represent this]. Ice is taken because it signifies cold congealment, which expresses "correct" (*zheng*). Nor is the color white taken [for this purpose]. A doubter asks:

"Why is the diagram's appearance black on the inside and white on the outside? Since all five diagrams use white to express 'partial' (*pian*), what is the intention behind this one alone expressing 'correct'?
One does not realize that the diagrammatic form of this position is subtle and profound, difficult to comprehend. Now, without begrudging the secret meaning, I shall clarify it further.
This is explained as follows: The circular form on the outside is constituted by the third yang line, an odd number, representing the central position.
The black form within represents the fourth yang line; its odd number likewise signifies the person within the central position.
This refers to taking the two yang lines as the odd numbers representing the dharma; it does not refer to the blank spaces within the circles.
However, regarding these five positions in the diagrammatic verses, only the first and last positions are free of error.

The three intermediate verses differ from the positions in the diagrams, and various editions diverge from one another without anyone having corrected them. Therefore, I have now set them forth here. Furthermore, I observe that [some] take the five positions as "ruler and minister."
It is likewise untenable to assign [the categories] to these five positions in their respective order;
for although both the "Ruler" (jun) and the "Minister" (chen) possess the five positions, their modes of expansion and contraction differ. Students should examine this with careful attention.

As for Linji’s Three Mysteries, Three Essentials, Four Guest-Master Dynamics, Four Modes of Discernment, and Four Aspects of Illumination and Function, each of these encompasses the matters within a single position. Thus one should know that the five...
The ultimate goal of this school is most vast and extensive; how could the establishment of any single tradition exceed this?

Next, taking the three lines of the outer hexagram as the "Samādhi of Receiving Use from Others" is because the fourth line represents a yang occupying a yin position, symbolizing the wondrous awakening that flows against the current and returns to enter the sea of birth and death, intending to arise from essence to manifest function by dividing its body.

Within the *dharmadhātu*, he universally responds according to the capacities of beings. Although he has not yet entered the secular world to benefit living beings, he has already mobilized great compassion and manifested hidden traces;
thus, this is different from the preceding hexagram-line and is represented by means of a yin position.

When a student reaches this stage, they have already realized the *dharmakāya* and are able to dwell neither in the realm of phenomena nor in the realm of formlessness; they do not cling to a state of barren stagnation, nor do they adhere to wordless silence.

This does not refer to one who seeks only personal liberation; rather, it refers to those who have vowed to leave behind their precious [attainments] to enter the mire and the water, performing great Buddha-work—this is what is assigned to this hexagram line.

If one aligns with the intent of the Patriarch, the yang lines of the preceding three positions represent yang at the culmination of its function and the extremity of its station, whereas this represents yang that turns its position toward the path of practice.
Viewing these two yang lines together, one is settled and still, while the other is darkly active; therefore—
This is because it is the coming from the very center. Therefore, it is said that at midnight, when the light is perfectly clear, one does not manifest at dawn.

Having reached these two stages, one’s self-benefit is already fulfilled; being naturally noble and venerable, one takes the dharma-realm and dharma-nature as one's body, thereby accomplishing the virtue of the Dharma-body.
Fearing that practitioners might become stuck at this point, he takes the middle two lines and interchanges them above and below to manifest the subtlety of the fruition-merit.
This is what is meant by "penetrating the source and penetrating the path," and "carrying along both the vehicle and the way."
The fifth line is old yin occupying the position of old yang. Its image represents the subsequent path of Samantabhadra’s perfected practice.

Having previously occupied that station, he rides upon his vows to engage the mundane world, manifesting transformation bodies according to the various types of beings; thus his great function extensively pervades the Dharma-realm. Therefore, while his essence is partial, his position is constant.

This is precisely the practice following the attainment of Buddhahood, sharing the same purport as the "Detachment from the World" chapter (*Lokadhātuparivarta*) of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Regarding this—

Within the five chapters on *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, this corresponds to "Tearing Apart the Great Net. If we consider it from the perspective of our Original Teacher, it represents the manifestation of turning the Great Dharma Wheel.
When the practitioner’s merit and wisdom are sufficient and the proper time has arrived, they take their seat, don their robes, and lay down their body for the sake of sentient beings.
On the vital path of the Mysterious Gate, one kills and gives life, seizes and releases; guest and host, ruler and minister, meet the opportunity and accord with the Way.

Those whose arrow-tips meet and whose pecking and hatching occur simultaneously are assigned to this rank. If one aligns this with the various patriarchs, this is one who has already penetrated the Dharma-body and acts as a model for beings;
thus, they are a "transformed birth. Because they do not abandon the causal gate after attaining the fruit, they remain like a prince. All...

The Dharma flourishes in tandem, and the myriad affairs of state proceed in unison; thus it is called "Shared Merit. Wondrously harmonizing with the universal path, where "knocking" and "singing" are raised together, it is therefore called "The Ultimate within the Simultaneous.
This is what the former sages, out of compassion, designated as the *dāna-pāramitā* (perfection of giving) of the Dharma.
The sixth line represents old yang occupying the position of old yin. Its image is that of the ultimate *dharmadhātu* sea of true suchness (*tathatā*).

While its essence is identical to that of the fourth line, their functions differ. The fourth line involves the essence engaging with function, whereas this [sixth line] involves subsuming function back into the essence.
Externally, it does not abide in the myriad practices; internally, it does not abide in the single mind. It is equal throughout the three periods of time and cuts off all directions at once.
Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings are utterly unobtainable—this is the Secret Treasury. Within the five chapters on *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, this corresponds to the "Great Abiding.
If we consider it from the perspective of our Original Teacher, it is the mark of his entry into parinirvāṇa; for the student, it is the single path to transcending the world.

When the task is completed, both the provisional and the ultimate are gathered together; the myriad functions are stilled, and one withdraws into a secure and profound seclusion, like a wild goat hanging from a tree branch—this is assigned to this stage.
If one aligns this with the various patriarchs, this is the school of the void, the profound, and non-attachment.
Returning to its source, it is of the same essence as the first stage; therefore, it is called "internal arising. There is no birth to be saved, and no world to be [transcended].
Arising is the ultimate state of non-action; thus it is the "functioning of non-function. Practice and position are simultaneously extinguished, falling neither into existence nor non-existence.
Reaching the ultimate limit of the present moment, one returns to the source and merges with the fundamental. Therefore, this is called "Arriving within the Simultaneous" (*jiānzhōngdào*).

As it is said: "Moving secretly and acting subtly, appearing as if ignorant and dull-witted. These two aforementioned stages, when expanded, traverse the entire Dharma-realm; when withdrawn, their footprints are difficult to find. This is—
Unfolding is immediately withdrawn; thought and deliberation are cut off. Because the four propositions and the hundred negations all fail to reach it, it constitutes the virtue of liberation.

Fearing that practitioners might not attain mastery upon reaching this point, the third layer’s two hexagrams are taken and interchanged above and below to exhaust the subtlety of the hidden and the manifest.
This is what is meant by: "Only being able to maintain continuity is called the Lord of Lords. Furthermore:
The first four lines represent the vow for the benefit of others; the fifth line represents the practice for the benefit of others;
and at this sixth line, the practice for the benefit of others is perfected, and one attains the sublime upon returning to the source. As the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states:

"Having established all my children within the secret treasury, I too shall not long remain outside, but shall abide therein myself. Therefore, these three lines together constitute the Enjoyment Body for Others (*para-sambhogakāya*).

This is samādhi. Question: Since the third line of the preceding inner trigram has already realized the ultimate fruit, one has reached the other shore of nirvāṇa and dwells within the secret treasury (guhyagarbha).
Having returned to the root and exhausted the source, there is no further progress. Now, is the realm reached by this sixth line the same as or different from that of the third?
If they are the same, how can the five stages be distinguished? If they are different, [how so?]
Then it should be even deeper. What is the meaning of this? Answer: The ocean of the nature of True Suchness (tathatā) originally has no two sources.

However, the former is the "Gate of the Original Source" returning to the source, while the present is the "Gate of Traces" returning to the source. Furthermore, the former represents the culmination of merit and the pinnacle of rank, where all human positions are correct;

the present represents the extinction of merit and the dissolution of rank, where all human positions are non-existent. Therefore, they are not the same. Thus, we know that Dongshan established [this].

Regarding the position: among the intermediate noble positions, he does not take the third line, which returns to the source, but takes the fourth line, which flows against the current, to establish the meaning of the position;
thus, the subtlety of the Patriarch’s intent is further revealed.
Furthermore, regarding the imagery of the six lines of this hexagram *Chongli* (Repeated Separation), if one investigates its beginning and end, it is a cycle without discernible starting point.
This is because the single true *dharmadhātu* is entirely devoid of traces; there is neither subject nor object, and it is fundamentally inexpressible.

When the two gates of principle (*li*) and wisdom (*zhi*) are first opened, principle becomes the "object realized" (*suo-zheng*) and wisdom becomes the "subject that realizes" (*neng-zheng*). Thus, the image of the first line arises; its diagram consists mostly of black and very little else.
It is said: "The predominance of black represents principle (li), while the scarcity of white represents wisdom (zhi).

This corresponds to the initial stage of abiding (zhùwèi), because at this point one has severed the first grade of the obstruction of ignorance regarding principle and possesses a single portion of the virtue of wisdom. Subsequently, wisdom opens the two gates of cause and effect; thus, the second and third lines (xiàng) arise.
The second line represents the cause, and the third represents the effect. The diagram of these two lines consists predominantly of white."
The area where black is minimal and white is predominant is the cause; the area where black is minimal [but present] is the fruit.
From this second stage onward, one realizes a portion of the true fruit within each successive position. Therefore, the three-line diagram is represented by a circle with a black mark inside.

This signifies that the ocean of the fruit has reached its ultimate limit and the causal stage is fully perfected; as wisdom merges with principle, it forms only a perfect circle. Next, the principle unfolds.
Regarding the two gates of essence (*tǐ*) and function (*yòng*), there arise the fourth and fifth lines (*xiàng*). The fourth is essence; the fifth is function.
Although the fourth line of essence encompasses function, it has not yet departed from the ocean of fruition; therefore, its diagram is the black mark within the preceding circle.
The fifth line does not abandon causal practice, and the great function manifests before one; its diagram is thus the mark of pure white. Within this white mark—

There is white and there is black; because it illuminates both white and black simultaneously, it becomes purely white. If it did not illuminate the black, it would not fulfill the meaning of "comprehensive arrival.

Having reached this point, it unfolds to its full extent and then retracts, subsuming essence and function into a single principle, merging cause and effect into a single wisdom, and gathering both principle and wisdom together to return to the one true Dharma-realm.
Therefore, the hexagram-line image of the sixth position arises. Its diagram is as follows: [diagram].
It constitutes the aspect of pure black. Within this aspect of black, there is neither black nor white; it is called "pure black" because both black and white have vanished together.
If black were not extinguished, it would not fulfill the meaning of "simultaneous arrival. Nevertheless, this one true *dharmadhātu* is ultimately ineffable;
it serves as the substance for the first stroke (*yāo*) and is fundamentally the primordial state where principle and wisdom (*jīli*) have not yet been divided.
Regarding that first stroke: at this point, it is said that even Vipaśyin was not yet enlightened, and how could Maitreya be so clearly aware?

Thus we know that, to speak of the essentials of the one hexagram with its six lines: the first line represents the initial opening of wisdom and principle; the sixth line represents the returning dissolution of wisdom and principle;
and the four middle lines represent the essence and function of cause and effect, revolving in a cycle from end to beginning, like a great round mirror.
If a student perceives this with a single glance and enters it with their whole being, then who is born? Who is a Buddha? What is the *zong* (essence) vehicle? What is the *jiao* (teaching) vehicle?
Furthermore, who belongs to the Dongshan school? Who belongs to the Linji school? Within a single light, the four modes of birth and the six realms of existence are present;
all sages and worthies are but a single reflection. This is like melting the gold of vases, plates, hairpins, and bracelets into a single mass.
Lu Cheng is one great round mirror. Then, having broken the mirror, there is nothing to be found.

This is what the *Lotus Sūtra* calls "ultimate nirvāṇa, the eternally quiescent mark," finally returning to emptiness. Let thousands of sages emerge and extensively establish their systems and principles;
they are all merely ghost-gates with talismans pasted upon them. Within this, there is not so much as a single character; what can you call it?
The Treasure Mirror Samādhi. It is said that the mere manifestation of patterns and colors belongs to defilement.
I bow my head to the Honored One of Pure Awakening, the Great Samādhi of the Treasure Mirror, and to all the worthies and sages of the Dongshan lineage as well as all the patriarchs:
may you each grant your secret seal, so that what I have spoken shall not deviate from the truth.
May all who study the profound mystery universally attain realization through seeing and hearing.
The Original Meaning of the Treasure Mirror Samādhi (Concluded).
